skill.name: benchmark-kernel
skill.description: Benchmark FlashInfer GPU kernels with CUPTI or CUDA event timing.
skill.summary: Guides accurate FlashInfer kernel benchmarking, backend comparison, reference checks, and CSV result capture.
skill.author: flashinfer-ai

security_audit.summary: The skill is benchmarking documentation with many Markdown command examples, most of which are false positives from code fences and inline command text. One real risk remains: it advises an optional sudo nvidia-smi command to disable GPU boost, which is legitimate for benchmarking but requires privileged host access.

remediation.suggestion: Add a warning before sudo nvidia-smi explaining that it changes host GPU state and should only be run on owned benchmark machines with administrator approval.

high_findings.confidence_reasoning: The skill recommends sudo nvidia-smi to lock GPU clocks. This is a privileged host command, so users should review it before running even though it supports legitimate benchmarking.

content.value_statement: GPU kernel benchmarks can be noisy when timing includes host overhead or inconsistent warmup. This skill guides Claude, Codex, and Claude Code through CUPTI timing, CUDA event fallback, reference checks, and repeatable result capture.
actual_capabilities: Explains when to use CUPTI timing and when CUDA events are an acceptable fallback.
Provides FlashInfer benchmark command patterns for attention, GEMM, and MOE routines.
Shows how to compare multiple backends such as FA2, cuDNN, CUTLASS, and TensorRT-LLM.
Guides reference checking, verbose output, reproducer command generation, and CSV result output.
Describes custom Python benchmarking with bench_gpu_time and common timing options.
Offers troubleshooting steps for CUPTI warnings, backend mismatches, unsupported backends, and noisy results.
limitations: Requires a local FlashInfer checkout and compatible GPU environment to run benchmarks.
CUPTI timing requires CUDA 13 or newer and the cupti-python package.
Does not automatically select safe benchmark dimensions for every GPU memory limit.
Includes an optional privileged GPU clock command that should be reviewed before use.

use_cases.title: Compare attention backends
use_cases.description: Run decode or prefill attention benchmarks across FlashAttention, cuDNN, CUTLASS, and TensorRT-LLM backends.

use_cases.title: Measure custom kernel timing
use_cases.description: Use FlashInfer timing helpers in a Python script to measure median runtime and variance for local kernels.

use_cases.title: Create reproducible benchmark reports
use_cases.description: Generate benchmark commands, reference checks, verbose diagnostics, and CSV output for sharing results with a team.

prompt_templates.title: Run my first benchmark
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner setup for a single FlashInfer benchmark.
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me run a first FlashInfer benchmark for decode attention. Explain the required flags, enable reference checking, and use CUDA events if CUPTI is not installed.

prompt_templates.title: Compare backend performance
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate benchmark comparison across supported backends.
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a FlashInfer benchmark command that compares FA2, cuDNN, and CUTLASS for my kernel shape. Include warmup iterations, measurement iterations, verbose output, and CSV output.

prompt_templates.title: Troubleshoot noisy results
prompt_templates.prompt: My FlashInfer benchmark has high standard deviation. Walk me through changes to warmup, iteration count, cache behavior, GPU clocks, and reference checks without changing the benchmark goal.

prompt_templates.title: Design a benchmark matrix
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced batch benchmarking for several kernels and backends.
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a FlashInfer benchmark test list for attention, FP8 GEMM, and MOE routines. Include backend choices, reproducibility settings, reference checks, and guidance for interpreting TFLOPS and bandwidth.

output_examples.input: I need to benchmark decode attention on H100 and compare three backends.
output: A recommended benchmark command with routine, backend, shape, dtype, iteration, and reference-check flags.
A short explanation of median time, standard deviation, TFLOPS, and memory bandwidth.
A reminder to save CSV output and generate a reproducer command.

output_examples.input: CUPTI is missing, but I still need useful timing results.
output: A clear explanation that CUDA events are the fallback timing method.
Steps to install CUPTI when CUDA 13 or newer is available.
Guidance on when CUDA event overhead matters for very fast kernels.

output_examples.input: My backends disagree during reference checking.
output: A diagnosis path for output mismatch errors.
Suggestions to inspect precision differences and verbose tensor statistics.
A caution that allowing mismatches should be a deliberate benchmark choice.

best_practices: Use reference checking when comparing backend performance so speed is not separated from correctness.
Record benchmark settings, output CSV files, and reproducer commands for every shared result.
Increase warmup and measurement iterations before drawing conclusions from noisy timing data.
anti_patterns: Do not compare backends without matching shapes, dtypes, and reference-check settings.
Do not treat CUDA event timing and CUPTI timing as identical for very short kernels.
Do not run privileged GPU clock commands on shared machines without approval.

faq.question: Does this skill require CUPTI?
faq.answer: No. It recommends CUPTI for the most accurate GPU timing, but FlashInfer can fall back to CUDA events.

faq.question: What benchmark routines does it cover?
faq.answer: It covers attention wrappers, FP8 and FP4 GEMM routines, and several MOE benchmark routines.

faq.question: Can it save benchmark results?
faq.answer: Yes. The documented workflow includes CSV output and reproducer command generation.

faq.question: Can it help debug incorrect backend outputs?
faq.answer: Yes. It explains reference check failures, precision differences, verbose diagnostics, and mismatch handling.

faq.question: Is the sudo command required?
faq.answer: No. The sudo nvidia-smi command is an optional advanced step for controlling GPU clocks during noisy benchmarks.

faq.question: Who should use this skill?
faq.answer: It is best for GPU performance engineers, CUDA developers, and ML infrastructure teams benchmarking FlashInfer kernels.
